Methods

No medical or research expert has reviewed this content yet. It is checked by AI tools and by the founder. An external medical or research reviewer is to be recruited once the site can be shown. Until then the grading rules below are applied as written, and they are a draft.

What this site is

ME Atlas gives an overview of the serious about what causes ME/CFS, and shows how much evidence stands behind each one. It describes the state of the evidence. It does not give treatment advice, and it does not say that an idea is right or wrong. Long COVID is marked on a hypothesis where the evidence overlaps. It is not a separate section.

Which hypotheses are listed

A hypothesis is listed when at least one study has data from an ME/CFS group defined by a recognised . The rule judges the method, not where an idea comes from. These are left out:

  • ideas with no peer-reviewed patient data yet;
  • studies of healthy people, animals or cells only (they can add background to a card, but cannot admit a hypothesis alone);
  • studies with no stated case definition cannot admit a hypothesis or count towards its level, because we cannot tell whether the patients had ME/CFS; a card may list them as other studies, for context;
  • claims backed only by opinion, anecdote, patient surveys without a clinical comparison, or material that is not peer-reviewed;
  • treatment products and commercial claims. The site lists hypotheses about causes, not remedies.

Hypotheses are not mutually exclusive. They may be links in one chain, or may apply to different groups of patients.

The evidence ladder

Draft — pending expert review. The bar for a hypothesis shows causal evidence, from rung 0 to rung 5. Grading follows only this published ladder; editors do not add criteria.

The six rungs
LevelNameWhat it means
0ProposedAn idea with a reasoned argument, but no direct patient data yet.
1First signsOne or more small or uncontrolled studies point towards it.
2Backed in a defined groupA controlled study in patients with a recognised case definition supports it.
3Repeated by othersAn independent group has reproduced the finding in a separate .
4Tested by interventionChanging the proposed factor changes the outcome in a controlled experiment, so the link goes beyond association.
5Causal case builtSeveral independent lines of evidence, including experimental evidence, together meet most of the , with no unresolved major contradiction.

A treatment that works is one kind of experimental evidence and can count towards level 4. It does not, on its own, confirm the root cause: a treatment can help without acting on the cause. Level 5 requires the whole causal case, not a treatment result.

What moves a hypothesis up or down

Up: a new study meeting the criteria of the next rung; an independent ; a better-defined cohort; a larger sample; a controlled design with a comparison group; a protocol.

Down or held back: failed replications; a finding that rests only on a broad case definition (Oxford-only cohorts) or a very small sample; no control group; no preregistration; results that conflict with equally strong studies (see "Contested evidence" below). A retracted study is removed from the evidence and the level is re-assessed.

Volume is not evidence. The number of papers, citations or news items never moves a hypothesis. Quality factors applied at every rung: case definition, sample size, controls, preregistration, conflicting results.

How the ladder maps to the Bradford Hill criteria

Where each criterion counts
CriterionWhere it counts
Strength of associationLevels 2–3
Consistency (repeated by different groups)Level 3
SpecificityLevels 2–5 (weighed, not required)
Temporality (cause comes before effect)Levels 4–5
Biological gradient (dose–response)Levels 4–5
Plausibility (a credible mechanism)Level 0 upward
Coherence (fits other knowledge)Levels 1–5
Experiment (change the factor, outcome changes)Level 4
AnalogyLevel 0–1 only; never enough to raise a level

Accepted case definitions

Every study on a card records the case definition used to decide who counted as a patient.

How each case definition is treated
Case definitionTreatment on the ladder
, , Accepted at every rung.
Accepted, flagged on the card as "does not require PEM".
(the 1988 CDC definition)Accepted like Fukuda: flagged on the card as "does not require PEM", ranked equal to Fukuda.
, version not statedAccepted like Fukuda and Holmes 1988, since neither CDC version requires PEM: flagged on the card as "does not require PEM", ranked equal to Fukuda. The card quotes the sentence that names the CDC criteria.
(only)Flagged as broad. Evidence resting only on Oxford-defined cohorts cannot raise a hypothesis above level 1.
None stated, or not yet checkedNot accepted. A card records which of the two applies, and for any named definition the sentence it was read from.

The two badges

Shown on every card, separate from the bar, each yes or no.

  1. Diagnostic marker validated in an independent cohort. Yes only when a measurable marker linked to the hypothesis has been tested in a second, independent patient group, with a stated case definition.
  2. Explains post-exertional malaise (). Yes only when at least one study at level 2 or above measures PEM directly (for example a repeated exercise test on two consecutive days, or a controlled exertion challenge with symptoms tracked afterwards) and links it to the hypothesis. The link must connect the proposed mechanism to the symptoms after exertion in the same patients; a measured change that is itself the hypothesised abnormality (for example a fall in oxygen use on the second test) does not on its own explain PEM. A cohort of ME/CFS patients alone is not enough.

Contested evidence

A level is contested when at least one study of comparable or higher quality contradicts the finding that supports it. Comparable quality means all three: the same or a stricter case definition (CCC, ICC and IOM 2015 rank above Fukuda and Holmes 1988, which rank equal and above Oxford), a control group, and at least half the sample size of the study it contradicts. Sample size here means the number of patients in the measurement that bears on the finding, not the whole study when only part of it was measured. A rung that rests on more than one study is contested when a study of comparable quality contradicts any study the rung needs.

  • Who decides: the founder, with the contradicting study linked on the card and the reason written in plain sentences, split into short paragraphs with their own sources when it needs more than two. AI may propose a conflict; it never sets one.
  • How it is shown: the bar is filled up to the highest uncontested rung; the rung or rungs under dispute are drawn as a hatched segment. The card lists both sides.
  • How it ends: a contested mark is removed when the conflict is resolved (for example a larger study settles it). The removal is recorded on What changed.

How content gets onto the site

This is the planned flow; most of it is not running yet. So far, papers are fetched with hand-run scripts, cards are drafted with AI help in supervised sessions and checked by a separate AI reviewer and by code that compares titles, years and case-definition quotes with the PubMed and Europe PMC records, and every level has been set by the founder. Nothing is published automatically.

Planned flow

The pipeline is planned to run mostly on AI, with mechanical checks in code and a human for high-impact changes and disputes.

  1. Weekly fetch. New papers will be fetched from PubMed and Europe PMC and the raw responses stored.
  2. Drafting agent. One AI agent will sort papers by hypothesis, extract study data (sample size, case definition) and write a draft card update. Each AI output will keep the source id it came from. The output is a draft only.
  3. Mechanical checks (code, not AI). Every cited id must exist in a fetched record; title, year and the case-definition quote are matched against that record; sample sizes are checked as a warning; every block of text must cite a source. A draft that fails is sent back to the drafting agent.
  4. Review agent. A second, independent AI agent will check the draft against the sources, the inclusion rule and the ladder. It will see the draft and the source records, not the drafting agent's reasoning.
  5. Second round. If the review agent rejects the draft, the drafting agent gets one revised attempt, which is checked again. If they still disagree after two rounds, the change goes to the founder.
  6. Decision by tier (below).
  7. Publication. Approved changes will be published in a weekly site update. The card shows when it was last checked and whether by the AI review pair or by the founder.
  8. Logging. Every published change gets an entry on What changed, with its date, card, reason, source and the tier that decided it. The log is public and kept permanently.
  9. Corrections. An error found later, including one reported by a reader, will be corrected the same way and logged as a correction.
Who decides what
TierChangeWho decides
1Adding a study to a card, factual text, change-log entryPlanned: published automatically when the mechanical checks pass and both agents agree. Not switched on yet; the founder approves every change.
2Setting or changing a level, a badge or a contested mark; adding or removing a hypothesisThe founder, yes or no, in a weekly list
3Anything still disputed after two agent roundsThe founder. If unresolved, the lower level stands and the disagreement is noted on the card

Until the founder rules the agents' error rate acceptable, the founder approves every change, including tier 1. That period has not started, because the pipeline is not running yet.

The role of AI, and who decides

AI drafts and checks. A human decides every level, badge, contested mark and new hypothesis. The content is checked by AI and by the founder and has not been reviewed by a medical or research expert.

Known limits

  • No medical or research expert has reviewed the content or the ladder yet.
  • The six rungs and their names have not been tested with readers.
  • Cards are only as complete as the searches run so far. A weekly search is planned but not running yet.

Explanations of the marked words on this page

A hypothesis is a proposed explanation that has not been settled. Here, an idea about what causes ME/CFS.
Checked by independent experts in the field before a scientific journal publishes it.
A written set of rules (symptoms, how long they have lasted, and illnesses that must be ruled out) used to decide who counts as having ME/CFS in a study.
A group of people followed or studied together.
Nine considerations from 1965 for judging whether a link between two things is likely to be causal, such as strength, consistency and whether the cause comes first.
Repeating a study, ideally by a different research group with new patients, to see whether the same result appears. A failed replication is a repeat that does not find it.
The plan for a study was filed publicly before it began, saying what would be measured and how it would be analysed. This makes it harder to change the question afterwards.
A 2003 case definition for ME/CFS. It requires six months of fatigue, worsening after effort, problems with thinking and, in most cases, sleep problems and pain, plus symptoms in other body systems.
A 2011 case definition for myalgic encephalomyelitis. It requires a marked worsening after effort and symptoms in several body systems, and has no six-month waiting period.
A 2015 case definition from the US Institute of Medicine. It requires six months of reduced activity with fatigue, worsening after effort and unrefreshing sleep, plus thinking or standing problems.
A 1994 case definition led by the US CDC. It needs six months of unexplained, disabling fatigue and four of eight listed symptoms. Worsening after effort is one of the eight, but not required.
The first US CDC case definition for chronic fatigue syndrome (1988). It needs six months of fatigue that halves activity, plus many listed symptoms. Worsening after effort is not required.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the US national public health agency. Its researchers led the 1988 (Holmes) and 1994 (Fukuda) case definitions for chronic fatigue syndrome.
A 1991 UK case definition that requires six months of disabling fatigue and no other specific symptom. It is broad, so a group chosen this way may include people who do not have ME/CFS.
Post-exertional malaise. Symptoms get worse after physical or mental effort that was manageable before. It often starts hours to a day or more later and can last days or longer.
